titulo.texto: The Image of Our Lady of Guadalupe

frase_gancho.texto: What the image shows and what it means to the faithful.

puente_narrativo.texto: Pause for a moment at the spot where the image is best seen.

guion_corto.texto: The image of Our Lady of Guadalupe depicts the Virgin Mary standing, with her hands joined and her head slightly bowed. She has brown skin and a blue-green mantle covered with stars. Rays of sunlight surround her, and beneath her feet there is a moon and an angel. For Catholics, she is the mother of Jesus, and that is why many people call her the Virgen Morena or the Morenita del Tepeyac. The Church teaches that honoring an image is not the same as worshiping it, because the honor is directed to the person represented. For millions of people, this image is a mother who accompanies, listens, and protects.

guion_largo.texto:
If you have already walked past the image, this stop is for looking at it more calmly and respectfully. And if you have not yet, it will help you know what to look for.

The first thing you see is the Virgin standing, with her hands joined and her head slightly bowed. Her face is serene, and her skin is brown. She wears a pink tunic with decorations and a blue-green mantle covered with stars. Around her there are golden rays, as if the light of the sun surrounded her. At her feet there is a moon and, beneath it, an angel who holds her up. At waist level she wears a dark band.

For centuries, the Catholic tradition has read these elements as signs. Many of the faithful see in the dark band a sign that the Virgin is expecting a child, Jesus. The rays of the sun wrap around her like a light. The joined hands and lowered gaze speak of prayer. For others, her brown face speaks of an encounter between peoples. Pope John Paul the Second called her the mestiza Virgin of Tepeyac. These are readings of faith. Each one is a way of looking at the image, not an official definition.

The Catholic Church teaches that honoring an image is not the same as worshiping it. The honor is directed to the person represented, who here is Mary, the mother of Jesus, whom Catholics recognize as the Son of God. When John Paul the Second canonized Juan Diego in this Basilica, he said that the Virgin revealed herself as the Mother of the true God. And he described her as a loving and compassionate mother who guides people to that God. That is the central idea of devotion to Our Lady of Guadalupe.

Over time, the popes have given Our Lady of Guadalupe various titles. In nineteen ten, Pius the Tenth named her patroness of Latin America. In nineteen forty-five, Pius the Twelfth called her Empress of the Americas. And in nineteen ninety-nine, John Paul the Second decreed that her feast day be celebrated on the twelfth of December throughout the continent.

The image has also been studied as a work of art. In seventeen fifty-one, the painter Miguel Cabrera and six other painters examined it closely. They wanted to describe its materials and its technique. Cabrera later published a book in which he maintained that the image was prodigious. Since then, many artists have made copies over the centuries.

Many other readings of the image also circulate, for example about the stars on the mantle or the eyes. Here we stay with what can be seen with the naked eye and with what the Church teaches.

For millions of people, this image is not just a work to look at. She is a mother. Some come to give thanks, some come to ask for help, and some come to be silent before her. If you do not share that faith, you can accompany them with respect. If you do share it, you can stay as long as you need.

texto: Find the blue-green mantle with stars
Look at the rays surrounding the Virgin
Notice the moon and the angel at her feet
